doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

title: Four-dollar gigs and the Italian wedding with Bucky Pizzarelli
summary: Igoe describes high-school dance-band jobs paying $4-5 and a wedding where Bucky's relatives took the stage and played unpaid.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well just before we started here you were talking about some of your early gigs with a good friend of Hamilton actually, Bucky Pizzarelli. He’s been up to the college a number of times.
And I like the stories about those four dollar gigs.
Oh, yeah. That’s all we made.
If you don’t mind just relating some of those, about the wedding?

Oh yeah when we were kids coming up in so-called musically, we were still in high school, and you know there was no rock & roll or Pop music as we know it today. It was all jazz and big bands, dance bands, you know like Vaughn Monroe, Jimmy Dorsey, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman. They were jazz players but they were primarily dance bands. And people danced to the music. And so when we were in high school, he was in Paterson, I was in Ridgewood, our paths didn’t cross yet. And I played with a band called Harry Comet. And jokingly we called it Harry Comet and his Meteorites. And when we played a job we made five dollars, and if we played a job on New Year’s Eve we might have made twelve for New Year’s Eve. Back then that was big money, in 1938, 1939. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Nobody had any money, the depression wasn’t even over yet. And that’s the way we learned to how to play, by playing all kinds of job. Now I think you were referring to the job about the wedding that came up? Bucky and I were playing an Italian wedding at a place called the Lafayette Friend’s Club in East Paterson. And I played there a lot, he played there a lot, sometimes we played together there. And this time we did. And I forget whose band it was. Anyway in those days the weddings were not glamorous like they are today. The caterer was a man who brought in barrels of sandwiches wrapped, and if somebody wanted a ham on rye they’d throw it, or throw me a turkey or a roast beef or whatever, and the booze was just keg beer, and everybody had a marvelous time. Everybody was dancing and having a marvelous time. And on this particular night I can remember still very clearly, we were playing along and all of a sudden these people start coming on the stage from both sides. And they were all Bucky’s relatives: his grandfather, his uncles, his cousins. And they all could play guitar or mandolin or something. So we did about a half an hour of Italian wedding stuff [scats]. And they loved it. And then they all disappeared. Nobody got paid. They just showed up and played and left. And so that’s the way it was back then.
I think I might have gotten four dollars on that job.
